title: Energy stores and transfers
examTip: You need to name stores exactly and describe transfers correctly. You also need to use Sankey diagrams to work out efficiency. Learn the eight stores and four transfer pathways by heart.
introTips: Learn the names of the energy stores. The names matter. Say 'kinetic', not 'movement'. Say 'gravitational potential', not 'height energy'.
Energy is never created or destroyed. It is transferred between stores, or dissipated. This is the law of conservation of energy. Every energy calculation you do is built on it.
Sankey diagrams are a common 2–3 mark question. The width of each arrow tells you the amount of energy. Here you will learn to read them and work out efficiency from them.
intro: Every time you move, eat, switch on a light or light a fire, energy is doing something. The way it is stored changes, or it is dissipated. But physics tells us the total never changes. Energy cannot be made from nothing, and it never disappears. Knowing where energy is stored and how it moves is the base of everything in physics. That includes engines, power stations, diet science and even climate change.

basics.text: Energy is what is needed to make things happen. It makes things move, heat up, light up or make a sound. You cannot see energy, but you can see what it does.
Energy is measured in joules, written J. One joule is a small amount, so big amounts are given in kilojoules (kJ). 1 kJ is 1000 J.
A store is somewhere things are kept until they are used. A piggy bank is a store for money. Energy can be kept in an object in different ways.
A force is a push or a pull. Kicking a ball and lifting a bag are both forces. Forces are measured in newtons (N).
An electric current is a flow of electric charge round a circuit. It is what makes a bulb light up or a phone charge.
Temperature tells you how hot or cold something is. It is measured in degrees Celsius (°C) with a thermometer. A hotter thing has a higher temperature.
If one thing is proportional to another, doubling one doubles the other. Twice as much energy means an arrow twice as wide.

keyPoints.heading: The eight energy stores
keyPoints.content: There are eight separate energy stores. You need to name them and give an example of each. - Kinetic: any moving object. For example, a car, a kicked ball or a running person. - Gravitational potential: any object raised above the ground. For example, a book on a shelf, or a roller coaster at the top of a hill. - Elastic potential: a stretched or squashed object. For example, a spring, a drawn bow or a squashed rubber ball. - Thermal: depends on an object's temperature. Every object has energy in its thermal store. A hot cup of tea has more than the same tea when cold. - Chemical: for example, food, fuels (petrol, wood) and batteries. - Nuclear: stored in the nuclei of atoms. For example, uranium, or the Sun's core. - Electrostatic: between charged objects. For example, static on a balloon, or the charge between a thundercloud and the ground. - Magnetic: between magnets or magnetic materials. For example, two magnets attracting or repelling.
writeBullets: Kinetic — any moving object
Gravitational potential — any object at height
Elastic potential — stretched or squashed objects
Thermal — every object. More energy at a higher temperature
Chemical — food, fuels, batteries
Nuclear — stored inside atomic nuclei
Electrostatic — between charged objects
Magnetic — between magnets

keyTerms.def: A way energy can be held. There are eight types: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear, electrostatic, magnetic
Energy stored in a moving object; calculated using Ek = ½mv², where m is mass (kg) and v is speed (m/s); measured in joules (J)
Energy stored in an object due to its height above a reference point; calculated using Ep = mgh, where g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth; measured in joules (J)
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed object; calculated using Ee = ½ke², where k is the spring constant (N/m) and e is the extension (m); measured in joules (J)

keyPoints.memTip: Use the acronym KGET-CNE-M: Kinetic, Gravitational, Elastic, Thermal, Chemical, Nuclear, Electrostatic, Magnetic. Picture a cheetah (kinetic) leaping off a cliff (gravitational). It lands on a spring (elastic) and heats up (thermal). It is powered by food (chemical), on a nuclear planet. It is struck by lightning (electrostatic) and hits a magnet (magnetic).

keyPoints.heading: The four ways energy is transferred
keyPoints.content: Energy does not just jump between stores. It is always transferred by a particular pathway. There are four main pathways: - Mechanically: by work done by forces, like pushing, pulling or kicking a ball. - Electrically: by work done when a current flows in a circuit. - By heating: energy flows from a hotter object to a cooler one (conduction, convection). Radiation is a separate pathway. - By radiation: by electromagnetic waves, such as light and infrared. Energy can also be carried by sound waves. The key wording is: 'energy is transferred [pathway] from the [store] store to the [store] store'. Practise that sentence.
writeBullets: Mechanically — by work done by forces
Electrically — by work done when a current flows
By heating — from a hotter object to a cooler one
By radiation — electromagnetic waves (light, infrared). Sound waves also carry energy

keyTerms.def: Energy transferred by work done by forces — e.g. pushing, pulling, kicking

keyTerms.term: Electrical transfer (work done when a current flows)
keyTerms.def: Energy transferred by work done when a current flows in a circuit
Energy transferred from a hotter object to a cooler one by conduction or convection; always flows from higher to lower temperature. Radiation is a separate pathway.
Energy transferred by electromagnetic waves, such as light and infrared

keyPoints.memTip: Energy is transferred by work done by forces, by work done when a current flows, by heating or by radiation. Practise the sentence: 'Energy is transferred [pathway] from the [store] store to the [store] store.'

keyPoints.heading: Conservation of energy — the rule that never breaks
keyPoints.content: The law of conservation of energy says that energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated (spread out). A system is an object or group of objects. The total energy in a closed system always stays the same. This is one of the most important laws in all of science. Say you push a book off a table. The gravitational potential energy does not disappear. It becomes kinetic energy as the book falls. When the book hits the floor, some energy is transferred by sound waves. It all ends up in the thermal store of the floor and surroundings. Track it, and you will always find the same total. When a system changes, energy moves between its stores. Common examples: - an object projected upwards: the kinetic store falls and the gravitational potential store rises - a moving object hitting an obstacle: the kinetic store falls and the thermal stores of both objects rise - an object accelerated by a constant force: work done by the force fills the kinetic store - a vehicle slowing down: the kinetic store falls and the thermal store of the brakes rises - water boiled in an electric kettle: energy is transferred electrically to the heating element. It is then transferred by heating to the thermal store of the water. Some is dissipated to the surroundings
writeBullets: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated
System — an object or group of objects
Total energy in a closed system is always constant
Energy that seems to 'disappear' has been transferred to thermal energy in the surroundings
Example: a falling book. Gravitational potential → kinetic → thermal store of the surroundings, partly transferred by sound waves

keyTerms.def: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated; total energy in a closed system is always constant
A system in which no energy is transferred to or from the surroundings — the total energy remains constant

keyPoints.memTip: Energy is NEVER created and NEVER destroyed. It only moves between stores or spreads out. Every energy question has the same total on both sides.

keyPoints.heading: Dissipation — where useful energy goes to die
keyPoints.content: In any real energy transfer, some energy ends up in a store that is no use. This is called dissipation. The most common dissipated form is thermal energy transferred to the surroundings. In other words, it is heat that warms the air around a machine. A car engine changes chemical energy in petrol into kinetic energy, which is useful. But some is transferred by sound waves (engine noise). This ends up in the thermal store of the surroundings. Some heats the exhaust and engine block. That energy is wasted. You are often asked to name the wasted energy store and explain why it is less useful. Wasted energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings, so it is stored in less useful ways. It becomes so spread out that it is harder to use. That spreading out is called dissipation.
writeBullets: Dissipation = energy spreading out into the surroundings, so it is stored in less useful ways
Most common wasted form = thermal energy transferred to the surroundings
Wasted energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings. So it is stored in less useful ways
Dissipated energy is harder to use, because it is spread out and at a low temperature
Example: a light bulb. Energy is transferred electrically to the bulb. It is transferred usefully by light (radiation). The rest is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings

keyTerms.def: The spreading of energy into the thermal store of the surroundings, making it less useful — most real energy transfers dissipate some energy
Energy transferred to a store that is not useful for the intended purpose of the device — most commonly dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings

keyPoints.memTip: Dissipation = energy spreading out and becoming less useful. Examiners may ask 'why is this energy less useful?'. Answer: it is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and cannot easily be recovered.

keyPoints.heading: Sankey diagrams and efficiency
keyPoints.content: A Sankey diagram is an arrow diagram. The width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy. The thick arrow on the left = total energy input. It splits into arrows on the right. One arrow = useful energy output. Other arrows = wasted energy, usually pointing down. The useful arrow is not always the widest. Worked example: a lamp is supplied with 100 J electrically. 15 J is transferred usefully by light. 85 J is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings. On a common scale, the input arrow is 100 units wide. It splits into a 15-unit arrow and an 85-unit arrow. 15 J + 85 J = 100 J, so the total is the same. Here the wasted arrow is wider than the useful one. To work out efficiency, use: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer. This gives a decimal. Multiply by 100 for a percentage. It is also written as: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input. A perfect device would have efficiency = 1.0 (or 100%). For most devices it is less, because some energy is dissipated. An electric heater is close to 1.0, because heating is its useful output.
writeBullets: Sankey diagram: arrow width = amount of energy
Thick left arrow = total energy input
Right arrow = useful output. Down arrow(s) = wasted energy. The useful arrow is not always the widest
Efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer
Multiply by 100 to get a percentage. For most devices it is less than 1.0 (or 100%)

keyTerms.def: A flow diagram where the width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy — the input arrow splits into useful output and wasted energy arrows
The ratio of useful output energy (or power) to total input energy (or power); efficiency = useful output ÷ total input; always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%)

keyPoints.memTip: Efficiency = useful OUT ÷ total IN. It is never more than 1. Wasted energy = input − useful output.

tables.title: The eight energy stores
rows: The object speeds up or has more mass
A skier at the top of a slope
The object is raised higher or has more mass
A compressed spring, a drawn bow
The object is stretched or compressed further
A hot cup of tea, engine exhaust gases
The object's temperature rises or it has more mass
More fuel or food is stored
Uranium fuel rods, the Sun's core
Opposite charges are pulled apart, or like charges are pushed together
Repelling magnets are pushed closer together, or attracting magnets are pulled further apart

0.question: A book sits on a high shelf. Which energy store does it have?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. The book is high up, so it has energy in its gravitational potential store. That would change to kinetic energy if it fell.
0.wrongFeedback: The book is high above the ground, so the correct store is gravitational potential. Kinetic needs movement. Elastic needs stretching or squashing. Chemical is the store in food or fuel.

1.question: A moving car brakes. Which pathway transfers energy from the car's kinetic store to the brakes?
options: Electrically. An electric current transfers energy to the brakes
By work done by forces. The friction force between the brakes and wheels does work to slow the car
By radiation. Infrared radiation carries energy from the car to the air
Chemically. The fuel reacts with brake fluid to release energy
1.correctFeedback: Correct. The friction force does work on the brakes, so energy is transferred mechanically. It ends up in the thermal store of the brakes and surroundings.
1.wrongFeedback: Energy can be transferred in four main ways. These are work done by forces, work done when a current flows, heating and radiation. Braking uses a friction force that does work. So energy is transferred to the brakes by work done by forces.

2.question: A student says energy is destroyed when a ball rolls to a stop on a carpet. Why is this wrong?
options: Energy is really created when the ball stops. It turns into cold
Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It has been transferred to thermal energy in the carpet and surroundings
The ball still has kinetic energy even though it has stopped
Energy is only destroyed if the object is on a frictionless surface
2.correctFeedback: Correct. This is conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed. When the ball stops, friction has transferred its kinetic energy to thermal energy (heat). That heat is in the carpet, the ball and the air around them.
2.wrongFeedback: Energy is never destroyed. The law of conservation of energy says total energy is constant. When the ball stops, its kinetic energy has been transferred to thermal energy (heat). That heat is in the carpet and surroundings. It has changed store, not disappeared.

3.question: A light bulb is supplied with 100 J of energy electrically. 15 J becomes light. The rest becomes thermal energy in the surroundings. Which term describes the 85 J of thermal energy?
options: Energy added to the bulb's chemical store
3.correctFeedback: Correct. The 85 J transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy is dissipated energy. It is no use for the bulb's purpose, which is light. It is spread out into the surroundings, where it is hard to recover.
3.wrongFeedback: Dissipation means energy transferred to a store that is no use for the job. Most often this is thermal energy spread out in the surroundings. The 85 J of thermal energy from the bulb is dissipated energy.

4.question: A motor is supplied with 500 J of energy electrically. It does 350 J of useful work. What is its efficiency?
4.correctFeedback: Correct. Efficiency = 350 ÷ 500 = 0.70 (or 70%). The other 150 J is dissipated, usually as thermal energy.
4.wrongFeedback: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input = 350 ÷ 500 = 0.70. If you got 1.43, you divided the wrong way round. Efficiency can never be more than 1. If you got 0.35, you divided by 1000 instead of 500.

commonMistakes: Kinetic energy belongs to moving objects. An object that is not moving has zero kinetic energy, however heavy it is.
Efficiency is always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%). If your answer is more than 1, you divided input by output. Divide output by input instead.

Wasted energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings, so it is stored in less useful ways. It is not 'destroyed'. If asked where wasted energy goes, say: transferred to the thermal energy store of the surroundings.
Sankey arrows that point down show wasted (dissipated) energy. The arrow pointing right (or forward) is the useful output. Find the right arrow before reading off values.
Gravitational potential energy goes up with both height AND mass. A heavier object at the same height has more GPE than a lighter one.
examTips: When describing an energy transfer, name the stores. Then say how the energy is transferred. It can be by work done by forces, by work done when a current flows, by heating or by radiation.

For Sankey diagram calculations, first read off the input and useful output values. Use the arrow widths or the numbers given. Then efficiency = useful output ÷ input. To find wasted energy: input − useful output.
You may be asked to 'explain why a device is not 100% efficient'. Say: some energy is dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings and cannot be recovered.
